title: The Last Innings? Inside the Growing Debate Over Rohit Sharma's Place in India's 2027 World Cup Plans
excerpt: Reports suggest chief selector Ajit Agarkar and coach Gautam Gambhir are not building their long-term ODI strategy around the 39-year-old former captain — but neither will they say so directly
body:
The question that Indian cricket's establishment would rather not answer out loud has finally been asked, and publicly. Is Rohit Sharma part of India's plans for the 2027 ODI World Cup in South Africa? And if so, will anyone tell him — or the country — in plain terms?

According to a report published this week by senior journalist Abhishek Tripathi, chief selector Ajit Agarkar and head coach Gautam Gambhir are "not currently considering" Rohit for the 2027 tournament. The selection committee is said to be closely monitoring his fitness and form before making any long-term commitment — a framing that, in the coded language of Indian cricket administration, often amounts to a soft exit strategy.

The former India captain turns 40 in April 2027, roughly six months before the World Cup is scheduled to begin across South Africa, Zimbabwe, and Namibia. He has already retired from Test cricket, announcing his departure in May 2025 after a bruising stretch that saw him average 10.93 in his final eight matches. He stepped away from T20 Internationals in June 2024, after captaining India to the T20 World Cup title. ODIs are his last format — and, in his own telling, his last chance at one more trophy.

## The numbers still work

It would be one thing if Rohit were fading quietly. But by statistical measures, the case for keeping him is not weak. He remains near the top of the ICC ODI rankings. In his most recent appearance, against Afghanistan in Chennai on June 20, he scored a fluent 79. In Australia earlier this year, he amassed 202 runs across three matches at an average of 101, including a match-winning century in Sydney that briefly returned him to the No. 1 ODI ranking at the age of 38.

His career record — 285 matches, 11,720 runs, an average of 48.83, and 33 centuries — belongs to a rarefied class. Only Sachin Tendulkar has scored more ODI runs for India. Rohit holds the all-time record for the highest individual ODI score (264, against Sri Lanka), the most double centuries in the format (three), and the most centuries in a single World Cup edition (five, during the 2019 tournament in England).

The problem, as it usually is with players of this stature, is not the present but the trajectory. His form dipped noticeably in the home series against New Zealand, where he managed just 61 runs at an average of 20.33. And the hard truth of sport at this level is that one bad tournament at 40 is the kind of risk selectors are increasingly reluctant to carry.

## The Manjrekar test

Sanjay Manjrekar, the former India batter and broadcaster, has articulated the dilemma as sharply as anyone. "If the selectors have picked Rohit, I hope it's because they genuinely see him as part of the 2027 World Cup plans," he told the Times of India. "We all know the culture around big-name players. Decisions are rarely as simple as judging on cricketing merit alone."

He went further: "If he is being picked because they are not ready to drop him, then it reflects a problem Indian cricket has had for years. Selection should never be about what's best for Virat, Rohit, or Bumrah. It should always be about what's best for Indian cricket."

It is a critique that lands because it names a truth everyone in Indian cricket can see but few will say: that the country's most celebrated players have historically been allowed to choose the timing of their departures, regardless of form or the team's needs.

## The Agarkar contradiction

Agarkar himself has been characteristically diplomatic. Speaking at the NDTV World Summit, he said Rohit and Virat Kohli would "not be put on trials" but also acknowledged that "2027 is a long way away" and that "we don't know what the situation is going to be."

In practice, the selectors have already acted. Shubman Gill has been appointed ODI captain, a decision Agarkar described as "difficult" but necessary because "at some stage you got to start looking at where the next World Cup is." Rohit was informed before the announcement — a courtesy that also signals finality.

"Even if he did not win the Champions Trophy as captain, it would have been a difficult decision because of how good he's been for India," Agarkar said. "But you've got to sometimes look at what's coming forward, where you stand as a team, and eventually look at what's in the best interest of the team."

## The quiet lobbying

Perhaps the most telling detail in recent reporting comes from the Times of India, which revealed that some senior players have directly approached top BCCI officials to seek clarity on their World Cup prospects — bypassing both Gambhir and Agarkar. The move suggests a disconnect between the management's public reassurances and the private signals players are receiving.

Former India all-rounder Yuvraj Singh echoed the frustration in an interview with Sports Tak. "I don't want any player who has represented the country for so long to be in a position where no one clearly communicates the plan to them," he said. "There should be an open discussion where you can sit down and talk honestly. Unfortunately, that kind of transparency isn't common in Indian cricket."

For the Indian diaspora, this debate carries a particular weight. Rohit Sharma has been the face of Indian cricket's golden age in the 50-over format — the captain who lifted the Champions Trophy in February 2025 in Pakistan, a campaign NRIs across the United States, Canada, and the United Kingdom followed with the kind of obsessive devotion that only Indian cricket can inspire. The idea that the Hitman might be eased out without ever being told — or that he might walk into an England dressing room in July not knowing whether it is his last series — unsettles fans who have watched him for nearly two decades.

The upcoming three-match ODI series in England, beginning July 14 at Edgbaston, now carries outsized significance. Every innings from Rohit will be read not just as a performance but as evidence — for or against the proposition that the Hitman has one more World Cup left in him.

Rohit's dream of one last World Cup is not dead. But the men who control the doors are already looking past him, even if they have not yet found the words to say so.
